entities.name: Darius the Mede
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Darius the Mede is a ruler named in the Book of Daniel as receiving the kingdom after the fall of Babylon and as the monarch under whom Daniel was cast into the lions’ den. The biblical text presents him as a Median king who organises the realm into satrapies and is manipulated by officials envious of Daniel. Outside Daniel, no clearly corresponding Median king of that name is attested in Achaemenid or Babylonian documentary sources for 539 BCE, when Cyrus the Great took Babylon.

Scholars have proposed identifications with figures such as Ugbaru/Gubaru (a governor associated with Babylon’s fall), Cyaxares, or a throne-name for Cyrus, or have treated Darius the Mede as a literary–theological construction that fits Daniel’s schema of successive empires. Regardless of historicity, the figure is central to Jewish and later Christian interpretation of the Exile’s end, divine sovereignty over empires, and the narrative of faithful witness under foreign rule. He thus matters as a biblical–historiographical problem at the intersection of Median memory, Achaemenid conquest, and Second Temple literature.
